A.title: UKGC Targets Illegal Operators' Funds, Not Just Websites
A.excerpt: The Gambling Commission has referred over £40m in suspected criminal funds since January and is moving against payments, suppliers and assets.
body: The Gambling Commission has signalled a decisive change in how it intends to fight the black market. In a statement issued on 9 November 2026, the regulator said it is widening its enforcement strategy beyond website disruption to target the funds, assets and commercial infrastructure on which illegal operators depend. The Commission reported that it has referred more than £40 million in suspected criminal funds to partner agencies since January 2026, with a view to those agencies pursuing asset freezing. Executive Director of Operations Sue Young framed the message bluntly, warning illegal operators that the Commission is coming after "you, your business and your money".

The headline numbers show the scale of the activity that preceded this shift. The Commission says it has issued more than 1,000 cease-and-desist notices in the 2026/27 year, referred more than 7.8 million URLs to search engines, secured the removal of more than 3 million URLs from search results and referred over 2,200 websites for disruption action. That work has been underpinned by government funding of £26 million over three years, with an initial £7 million made available from April 2026. The new emphasis on money rather than domains reflects a widely shared view that URL takedowns alone cannot keep pace with mirror sites and rapidly rotating brands.

The legal architecture for a money-focused approach already exists. Providing facilities for gambling in Great Britain without an operating licence is a criminal offence under section 33 of the Gambling Act 2005, and the proceeds of that activity are capable of being criminal property for the purposes of the Proceeds of Crime Act 2002. That framework gives law enforcement access to account freezing orders, cash seizure and forfeiture, and confiscation following conviction. The Commission does not itself hold most of those powers, which is why its strategy is built around referrals to partner agencies and close working with police on cash seizures at illegal land-based premises.

The more consequential part of the announcement for the licensed industry is the focus on commercial infrastructure. The Commission says it intends to obstruct payments and advertising and to stop illegal operators obtaining the games and sportsbooks that their businesses rely on. In practice, that places B2B suppliers, payment service providers, affiliates and marketing partners at the centre of enforcement. Licensed software suppliers are already prohibited from supplying unlicensed operators targeting British consumers, and recent enforcement rounds have shown the Commission is willing to pursue suppliers whose content surfaces on black-market sites. The latest statement makes clear that supply-chain leakage will be treated as a priority rather than a technicality.

Further tools are on the way. In an October 2026 speech, Chief Executive Sarah Gardner referred to forthcoming powers that would allow the Commission to apply to the courts for IP and domain-name suspension orders. If enacted in the form described, those orders would give the regulator a judicial route to compel action by registries and infrastructure providers, rather than relying on voluntary cooperation from search engines and hosting companies. Operators and suppliers with complex group structures should expect the evidential record built through current referrals to be used in support of such applications once the powers are in force.

For licensees, the practical implications fall into three areas. First, supplier and B2B licensees should review distribution contracts, white-label arrangements and API access controls to ensure their content cannot be accessed by unlicensed sites serving British customers, and should be able to evidence that review. Second, operators and payment partners should revisit transaction-monitoring rules for merchant activity that may indicate black-market gambling, since early reporting and intelligence sharing are explicitly named as critical by the Commission. Third, affiliates and media partners should audit their portfolios for unlicensed brands, because advertising pathways are now an express enforcement target.

The Commission's shift also has a policy dimension. Its recent research on illegal gambling engagement has been cited on both sides of the debate about whether licensed-market restrictions push consumers offshore. By attacking the economics of illegal operation rather than only its visibility, the regulator is positioning enforcement as a counterweight to arguments that tighter licensed-market rules inevitably feed the black market. Firms that can demonstrate robust supply-chain controls are likely to find themselves on the right side of that argument, while those with weak controls face a growing risk of regulatory action and reputational damage.

A.title: Texas HJR 52: Ten Casinos, 15% Tax Cap, No iGaming
A.excerpt: A new Texas resolution would allow up to 10 land-based casinos and cap gaming tax at 15%, while leaving mobile sports betting to lawmakers.
body: Texas gambling expansion is back on the legislative agenda. On 9 November 2026, the first day on which bills could be pre-filed for the 2027 regular session, Representative Charlie Geren filed House Joint Resolution 52, a proposed constitutional amendment that would authorise up to 10 casinos in the state. Senator Carol Alvarado filed a Senate companion, SJR 11. Because the Texas Constitution prohibits most forms of gambling, any meaningful expansion must proceed by joint resolution, approved by two-thirds of each chamber and then ratified by voters. If both chambers pass the measure, it would go to a statewide election on 2 November 2027.

The structure of HJR 52 is deliberately narrow on casino gaming. Each initial casino licence would run for at least 40 years, a term designed to support the capital investment that destination resorts require. Crucially, casino gaming would be limited to on-site play at the licensed operator's physical premises. That language would constitutionally exclude online casino gaming, making Texas a land-based-only casino jurisdiction unless the constitution were amended again. For iGaming operators hoping that the largest unregulated US market might eventually open to online slots and table games, HJR 52 offers little encouragement.

Sports betting is treated differently. The resolution imposes no on-site restriction on sports wagering and leaves the Legislature to determine where bets may be placed, including whether mobile wagering is permitted. That drafting choice matters. It means that if voters ratify the amendment, the battle over the shape of the Texas sports betting market, including the number of mobile skins, eligible licensees and any tethering to land-based or professional sports venues, would move to ordinary enabling legislation, which requires only simple majorities.

The fiscal terms will attract equal attention. HJR 52 caps the tax on casino and sports betting revenue at 15% and bars additional taxes or fees aimed specifically at gaming revenue. Embedding a tax ceiling in the constitution is unusual and would offer operators a degree of fiscal certainty that is absent in states such as Illinois, Ohio and New Jersey, where sports betting and gaming tax rates have been raised by statute after launch. For investors modelling a Texas entry, a constitutional cap of 15% would materially reduce the risk of post-licensing tax escalation.

The resolution also adds a subsection to Article III, Section 47 of the Texas Constitution and requires tribal gaming compacts, an acknowledgement of the federal Indian Gaming Regulatory Act framework and of long-running litigation involving Texas tribes. The Senate companion goes further on institutional design by creating a gambling regulatory commission, funded from lottery proceeds and gaming taxes and fees, with investigative and enforcement powers. The interaction between a new commission, the Texas Lottery Commission and existing tribal arrangements will be a key drafting issue if the measure gains momentum.

The political obstacles remain significant. The Legislature convenes on 12 January 2027, and the House Speaker will not refer HJR 52 to a standing committee before then. Geren's 2025 equivalent, HJR 137, was referred to the House State Affairs Committee in March 2025 and never advanced. The two-thirds threshold in both chambers is demanding, and Senate leadership has historically been the principal barrier to gambling expansion in Texas. Stakeholders should therefore treat HJR 52 as an opening position in a long negotiation rather than a likely 2027 outcome.

Even so, the filing is useful for operators, suppliers and investors because it sets the parameters of the debate early. Businesses interested in Texas should be engaging now on licence allocation, suitability standards and the design of the regulatory commission, and should be preparing coalition strategies with tribal, racing and professional sports stakeholders. Companies whose interest is primarily in iGaming should recognise that the on-site language in HJR 52 would foreclose that opportunity at a constitutional level, and that any intervention on that point needs to happen before the text is fixed for the ballot.

A.title: CFTC Warns Kalshi Over Contract Self-Certification
A.excerpt: Kalshi has reportedly been warned of possible CFTC charges over how it notified dozens of new contracts. Self-certification is now in focus.
body: The Commodity Futures Trading Commission has reportedly warned Kalshi that it could soon face enforcement charges. According to reporting by Politico on 10 November 2026, later echoed by Reuters, the agency is investigating whether the prediction-market exchange failed to properly notify it about dozens of new products before listing them. No charges have been filed and Kalshi's contracts remain live. A Kalshi spokesperson described the matter as a procedural error involving a handful of contracts, many of which were never live, and said the company is already addressing it.

The case goes to the heart of how prediction markets have scaled. Designated contract markets may list new contracts by self-certifying to the CFTC that the product complies with the Commodity Exchange Act and the Commission's regulations, under the procedures in Part 40 of the CFTC rules. Self-certification allows an exchange to launch a contract without prior approval, subject to the CFTC's ability to stay or review it. Kalshi has relied heavily on that route since its 2024 court victory over the agency, and the speed with which it has rolled out sports and event contracts has depended on it.

The CFTC has been signalling discomfort with how that pathway is being used. In July 2026, the Division of Market Oversight reportedly advised exchanges against using a single broad certification to cover many contracts, a warning said to have named Kalshi and Polymarket. A separate June proposal would introduce a 90-day review window for new contracts. Taken together with the reported pre-charge warning, these steps suggest that the agency views the integrity of the certification process, rather than the legality of event contracts as such, as its strongest enforcement lever.

That distinction matters for the wider industry. Much of the public debate about prediction markets has centred on federal pre-emption of state gambling laws, with courts in New York, Nevada, Michigan and elsewhere reaching different conclusions on whether CFTC jurisdiction displaces state regulation. A filing-procedure case avoids those questions entirely. It tests whether an exchange has complied with the federal regime on its own terms, and a finding against Kalshi would be difficult to characterise as an attack on the product category. For exchanges that have positioned federal oversight as the answer to state objections, that is an uncomfortable line of attack.

The warning also lands amid an unusually busy period of federal and state action. On 5 November, the CFTC said that federally regulated prediction markets generally cannot block traders by state, giving exchanges 30 days to comply. Kalshi's sports contracts are blocked in Michigan, Nevada and Washington, and it withdrew them from Utah after state prosecutors filed criminal charges against the company and its co-founders. On 4 November, a federal judge ordered Kalshi to block sports contracts on California tribal lands. The CFTC is also reported to be examining Polymarket's compliance with its 2022 settlement requiring it to block US users.

For exchanges, brokers and intermediaries offering event contracts, the immediate compliance lesson is that product governance must be documented contract by contract. Certification submissions should be specific, accurate and filed before launch, and internal controls should prevent products going live, even briefly or in test form, without a completed filing. Exchanges that have used template or omnibus certifications should consider whether re-filing or voluntary engagement with the Division of Market Oversight is prudent before any formal rule change or enforcement precedent fixes the standard.

For sportsbooks and casino operators watching from the licensed gambling side, the development is a reminder that the regulatory contest over prediction markets is not only being fought between states and the federal government. The federal regulator is itself tightening its expectations, and an enforcement case against the largest US event-contract exchange would sharpen the compliance cost of operating under the CFTC model. Operators considering partnerships with, or investment in, prediction-market platforms should factor federal enforcement exposure into their due diligence alongside the state-law risks that have dominated discussion to date.

A.title: New Zealand Online Casino Licences: 1 December Cut-Off
A.excerpt: Unlicensed online casinos must exit New Zealand on 1 December 2026 unless they have applied. Eleven auction winners now face suitability checks.
body: New Zealand's transition to a licensed online casino market reaches its most important deadline in less than three weeks. Under the Online Casino Gambling Act 2026, which came into force on 1 May 2026, providers that have not applied for a licence must stop offering online casino gambling to New Zealanders from 1 December 2026. Applicants may continue to operate, without advertising, until their applications are determined, but declined applicants must exit the market. The Department of Internal Affairs expects the licensed regime to be fully operational in 2027.

The licensing model is one of the most tightly capped in the world. A maximum of 15 licences is available, each covering a single brand. Licences have an initial term of up to three years and may be renewed for a further five years, and no entity may hold more than three. Rather than allocate licences on merit alone, the government ran an ascending clock auction between 29 September and 12 October 2026. The auction attracted 32 bidders, ran for 10 rounds and closed at a price of NZD 15 million per licence. Eleven entities secured the right to apply, with Baytree Interactive holding rights to three licences and Playvia Gaming and Rock Swift Group holding two each.

The auction result is not the end of the process. The Department has been explicit that success in the auction does not guarantee that a licence will be granted. Applications opened on 20 October 2026 for successful bidders, who must pay the auction-determined amount and submit a business plan together with strategies covering advertising, consumer protection, harm prevention and compliance. The Secretary for Internal Affairs cannot grant a licence without being satisfied that the applicant is suitable. For bidders that have paid a substantial sum for the right to apply, the suitability stage carries real commercial risk.

Suitability reviews in a newly regulated market tend to focus on corporate structure, source of funds, beneficial ownership and the applicant's regulatory history in other jurisdictions. Groups with a track record of serving New Zealand customers from offshore licences, including from Malta and other European hubs, will need to present that history carefully. Applicants should expect questions on past advertising practices, complaints, sanctions and the operation of affiliated brands that will not be licensed, and should ensure that disclosures are consistent with filings made to other regulators.

The transitional rules impose immediate operational constraints. Online casino advertising is prohibited for now, no new providers may enter the market before the 2027 launch, and only providers that were operating as at 1 May 2026 may continue under the transitional provisions. Operational regulations were released on 4 June 2026 and Minimum Standards on 8 July 2026, so applicants already have the technical and player-protection framework against which their systems will be assessed. Gaps between current offshore operations and those Minimum Standards should be closed before licence decisions are made, not after.

The cap of 15 single-brand licences also has significant consequences for the wider supply chain. Multi-brand groups must choose which brands to put forward and plan the orderly closure of others serving New Zealand. Affiliates and marketing partners face a market in which only a small number of licensed brands can advertise once restrictions are lifted. Game studios and platform providers should be mapping which of their customers hold auction rights, because supplying unlicensed operators after the cut-off is likely to attract regulatory scrutiny in New Zealand and elsewhere.

New Zealand's model is worth close study beyond its borders. Combining an auction for scarce licences with a full suitability assessment and strict transitional limits is a distinctive approach that differs sharply from the open licensing models used in much of Europe and the ring-fenced state-operator approach still dominant in parts of the Nordics. With Australia continuing to prohibit online casino gaming at the federal level, New Zealand's experience in 2027 will be a closely watched test of whether a capped, high-price licensing market can channel players away from offshore sites.

A.title: Denmark Gambling Bill: Live-Sport Ad Ban and New Powers
A.excerpt: Denmark's reform bill brings a whistle-to-whistle betting ad ban, warrantless inspections and revenue-linked fines, phased in during 2027.
body: Denmark is moving ahead with one of the most significant overhauls of its gambling framework since the market opened to licensed online competition in 2012. On 7 October 2026, Minister for Taxation Jakob Engel-Schmidt presented to the Folketing a bill implementing the reform package known as Spilpakken 1, first made public in October 2025. The bill reintroduces the substance of an earlier version that lapsed when an election was called. Implementation is planned in phases between January and October 2027, giving operators a narrow window to adapt advertising, player-protection and land-based operations.

The advertising measures will attract the most attention. The bill bans gambling marketing aimed at minors or featuring anyone under 25, prohibits gambling advertising on public transport and within 200 metres of schools and youth education institutions, and introduces a so-called whistle-to-whistle restriction on betting advertising during live sport. That restriction runs from ten minutes before kick-off until ten minutes after the event ends and covers screens, streams and in-play odds. The live-sport measures are scheduled to take effect in July 2027. Unauthorised gambling marketing would also become a criminal offence.

The inclusion of in-play odds within the advertising restriction is a notable drafting choice. In several European markets, odds displays integrated into broadcasts and streams have been treated as a grey area between editorial content and advertising. By naming them expressly, the Danish bill brings those integrations clearly within scope. Operators with media partnerships, sponsorship arrangements involving live broadcast inventory or odds-integration deals with streaming platforms should review those contracts now, since the July 2027 start date will fall in the middle of many multi-season agreements.

On player protection, the bill requires licence holders to monitor player behaviour in real time and to intervene when they detect signs of harm. Danish licensees already operate under duty-of-care expectations, but placing real-time monitoring on a statutory footing raises the evidential bar. Operators should expect the Danish Gambling Authority to test not only whether detection models exist, but whether they trigger timely, documented interventions. That mirrors the trajectory of supervision in Sweden, the Netherlands and Great Britain, where regulators have increasingly sanctioned operators for failing to act on risk indicators already visible in their own data.

Enforcement powers are strengthened considerably. The Danish Gambling Authority would gain powers to carry out inspections of suspected illegal operators without a court warrant, and fines would scale with company size and annual gross gaming revenue. In serious cases, imprisonment of up to one year would be available. Revenue-linked fines represent a meaningful change for a regulator whose sanctions have historically been modest by comparison with those imposed in the Netherlands or Great Britain, and they will sharpen the commercial risk of compliance failures for larger groups.

The land-based sector faces structural change. The bill replaces the existing manager approval model with a new dealer licensing regime covering lotteries, bingo, betting, casino games and gaming machines. Revised definitions for gaming shops and gaming halls require physical separation, staffing throughout opening hours and the exclusion of minors. Fast-paced games would be restricted to the hours between 7am and midnight, and new or combined game variants would require explicit regulatory approval. Retail operators and machine suppliers should plan for licensing applications and premises adjustments well ahead of their relevant commencement dates.

The government's own figures acknowledge a fiscal cost, with the advertising limits projected to reduce state revenue by DKK 15 million in 2027 and DKK 25 million annually thereafter, and the regulator expected to lose DKK 1 to 2 million in licensing fees. Industry critics have questioned whether the evidence supports the advertising restrictions. Whatever the outcome of that debate, the direction of travel is clear. Operators licensed in Denmark should be preparing implementation roadmaps now, aligning Danish controls with group-wide Nordic compliance programmes and engaging with the parliamentary process while the detail of the phased timetable remains open.
